'''Donald Alfred Gurnett''' (April 11, 1940 – January 13, 2022) was an American physicist and professor at the [[University of Iowa]] who specialized in [[Plasma (physics)|plasma physics]].<ref name="auto">{{cite web |url=https://now.uiowa.edu/2022/01/legendary-iowa-space-physicist-donald-gurnett-dies |title=Legendary Iowa space physicist Donald Gurnett dies |date=January 13, 2022 |website=Iowa Now |access-date=January 29, 2022}}</ref><ref name=press-citizen>{{cite news |url=https://press-citizen.com/obituaries/icp022841 |title=Donald Alfred Gurnett Obituary |work=[[Iowa City Press-Citizen]] |access-date=January 18, 2022}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Gurnett grew up in [[Fairfax, Iowa]]. In his spare time, he built and flew model airplanes with a club at the airport in Cedar Rapids. There, he met the German expatriate scientist [[Alexander Lippisch]].<ref name="auto"/>

Gurnett received his bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the University of Iowa in 1962, and then his master's degree in physics in 1963 and his doctorate in 1965.<ref name="auto"/>

==Career==
Gurnett's research into space plasmas (and his involvement in the development of electronics and measuring devices for space missions) began while he was a student, and eventually led to early studies of [[plasma waves]] in the Earth's [[Van Allen radiation belt|radiation belt]] (via low-frequency radio waves).<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gurnett|first=D.|date=October 1, 1974|title=The Earth as a radio source: Terrestrial kilometric radiation|url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1029/JA079i028p04227|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research|language=en|volume=79|issue=28|pages=4227–4238|doi=10.1029/JA079i028p04227|bibcode=1974JGR....79.4227G|url-access=subscription}}</ref> From 1962, he was a [[NASA]] trainee at the University of Iowa and [[Stanford University]] (1964/65). He participated in the [[Injun (satellite)|Injun satellites]] program, designed and built by researchers at the [[University of Iowa]] to observe various radiation and magnetic phenomena in the [[ionosphere]] and beyond.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Don Gurnett images|url=https://space.physics.uiowa.edu/~dag/images/index.html|access-date=February 6, 2022|website=space.physics.uiowa.edu}}</ref>  In 1965, he became an assistant professor, in 1968 an associate professor, and in 1972 a professor at the University of Iowa.<ref name="auto"/>

He was involved into 41 NASA missions, including [[Voyager program|Voyager mission]] to the outer planets,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gurnett|first1=D. A.|last2=Kurth|first2=W. S.|last3=Scarf|first3=F. ==Awards and honors==
In 1998, Gurnett became a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://physics.uiowa.edu/people/donald-gurnett|title=Donald Gurnett, Ph.D. &#124; Physics and Astronomy - The University of Iowa|website=physics.uiowa.edu|access-date=January 18, 2022|archive-date=January 18, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220118232738/https://physics.uiowa.edu/people/donald-gurnett|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2004, he became a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/donald-gurnett|title=Donald A. Gurnett|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |access-date=January 29, 2022}}</ref>

In 2006, he received the EGU Hannes Alfvén Medal. In 2014 he gave the Van Vleck Lecture. He was also awarded the [[Humboldt Prize]], with which he was at the [[Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics]] in Garching (1975/76). In 1989 he received the John Adam Fleming Medal from the [[American Geophysical Union]] and the Excellence in Plasma Physics Award from the [[American Physical Society|APS]] and in 1978 the John Howard Dellinger Gold Medal from the [[International Union of Radio Science]]. In 1979/80 he was a visiting professor at UCLA.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.egu.eu/awards-medals/hannes-alfven/2006/donald-gurnett/|title=Donald A. Gurnett|website=European Geosciences Union (EGU) |access-date=January 29, 2022}}</ref>

==Personal life ==
He was married to his wife Marie. Together they had two daughters, Suzanne and [[Christina Gurnett|Christina]].<ref name=press-citizen/>

Gurnett died on January 13, 2022, at the age of 81.<ref name=press-citizen/>
